title: Open/Closed Principle
summary: Open for extension, closed for modification — how polymorphism lets you add behavior without editing code that already works.

slides.markdown:
The **Open/Closed Principle** (OCP) says a module should be **open for extension, but closed for modification** — you should be able to add new behavior without editing code that already works and is already tested.

Think of a power strip: adding a new appliance means plugging into an open socket, not rewiring the strip itself. This topic covers what "closed" actually protects, and the polymorphism trick that makes "open" possible.

slides.sectionTitle: OCP defined: open for extension, closed for modification
slides.markdown:
**Open for extension** means new behavior can be added as the system grows. **Closed for modification** means adding that behavior shouldn't require editing existing, already-shipped source files.

The two halves aren't in tension — they describe the same design from two sides. A `PaymentProcessor` interface with a `CreditCardProcessor` implementation is closed: nothing about the interface or the existing implementation needs to change. Adding `PayPalProcessor` as a new implementation is the extension: new code, zero edits to old code.

OCP is a design goal for the boundaries you expect to grow, not a rule to apply to every class up front.

slides.sectionTitle: Why "closed for modification" protects already-tested code
slides.markdown:
Every edit to a shipped, tested file is a chance to reintroduce a bug that was already fixed once. If adding a new payment method means adding an `else if` branch inside an existing `processPayment()` method, every new branch re-risks every path that already worked — a typo in the new branch's condition can silently break the old ones.

OCP's real payoff is regression safety: when extension happens through new files implementing a stable interface, the git diff for adding a feature touches zero lines of previously-shipped, previously-tested code. Old tests keep passing because old code didn't move.

The existing `Shape` interface and its `Circle`/`Rectangle` implementations never change when `Triangle` is added — the new class simply plugs into the same contract, and any code that already calls `shape.area()` works on it with zero edits.

How OCP leans on abstraction and polymorphism to work
slides.markdown:
OCP isn't achievable through discipline alone — it needs a language mechanism that lets one call site work against many implementations without knowing which one it's talking to. That mechanism is **polymorphism**: code calls `shape.area()` through the `Shape` abstraction, and the right implementation runs based on the actual object, not a type check the caller wrote.

Without an abstraction to extend behind, there's nothing to be "open" through — you'd be back to branching on type inside one function, which is exactly the closed-for-modification violation OCP is naming.

OCP can be achieved two common ways, and picking the wrong one creates its own rigidity:

| | Inheritance-based | Strategy/plugin-based |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Subclass overrides a base class's method | Object holds a reference to an interchangeable interface implementation |
| Extension point | Fixed at compile time via subclassing | Can be swapped at runtime (config, DI container) |
| Risk | Deep hierarchies get brittle (see LSP) | Slightly more upfront wiring (an interface + injection) |
| Good fit | A true is-a relationship with shared structure | Behavior that varies independently of the object's identity |

**How to decide:** if the behavior might need to change at runtime or mixes independently of the object's type (e.g. pricing strategy, payment method), prefer strategy over inheritance.

**Wrong belief:** "OCP means I should add an abstraction and extension point for everything now, in case we need to extend it later."

**Why it's wrong:** an interface with exactly one implementation and no concrete plan for a second one is pure overhead — an extra layer of indirection to read through, for a future that may never arrive. This is **speculative generality**, and it makes code harder to follow while providing zero present benefit.

**Correct model:** apply OCP where variation is already happening or clearly imminent (a second payment method is already on the roadmap), not everywhere. Refactor a concrete class into an abstraction when the second real case shows up, not before.

slides.sectionTitle: Where OCP shows up in framework design: hooks, plugins, middleware
slides.markdown:
OCP is the principle behind almost every extensibility mechanism you use daily. Express and Koa let you add behavior via **middleware functions** without editing the router's core dispatch code. WordPress and browsers expose **hooks** and **extensions** so third parties add features without patching the host application. Test frameworks expose **plugin** interfaces so a new reporter or assertion library doesn't require forking the runner.

Recognizing this pattern helps in interviews: when asked to design something "extensible," naming a concrete hook/plugin/middleware point is a much stronger answer than saying "I'd use good OOP."
